Q: How can I write a regex that can find passwords in texts and binary data? A:

Your mission statement was to find passwords in binary stream. You can parse a binary stream but the data as seen by the regex engine is 1 byte per character. That's 0-255 decimal - the byte. That's the ascii / extended ascii ranges. Any password characters would only be discernible as a byte. So in binary, ascii strings are packed sequences of 8-bit binary. There is no decoding into Unicode because those characters are > x100. So you are restricted to ascii. Moreover, you can only match printable sequences between x21-x7e to be a realistic non-whitespace password. With that in mind you could try using just hex constructs \xdd :

(?<![\x21-\x7e])(?=[\x21-\x7e]{0,500}[a-z])(?=[\x21-\x7e]{0,500}[A-Z])(?=[\x21-\x7e]{0,500}[0-9])(?=[\x21-\x7e]{0,500}[\\!-#%-*,-/:;?@\[\]_{}])([\x21-\x7e]{10,501})

expanded

(?<! [\x21-\x7e] )
(?= [\x21-\x7e]{0,500} [a-z] )
(?= [\x21-\x7e]{0,500} [A-Z] )
(?= [\x21-\x7e]{0,500} [0-9] )
(?= [\x21-\x7e]{0,500} [\\!-#%-*,-/:;?@\[\]_{}] )
( [\x21-\x7e]{10,501} )       # (1)

Q: Inconsistent nonzero: pandas sparse and dense arrays A:

Clearly, the sparse and dense arrays don't differ in only an internal way, as you don't get the same thing after a round trip:

Sparse and dense arrays have a pretty important difference: sparse arrays have multiple representations of an array of zeros. Dense arrays have only one representation.

For example, in this code, a and b have different internal representations, but the same semantic meaning.

import pandas as pd
from pandas._libs.sparse import IntIndex
sparse_index = IntIndex(3, np.array([0, 1, 2]))
a = pd.arrays.SparseArray([0, 1, 2], sparse_index=sparse_index)
sparse_index = IntIndex(3, np.array([1, 2]))
b = pd.arrays.SparseArray([1, 2], sparse_index=sparse_index)
print(a)
print(b)

Output:

[0, 1, 2]
Fill: 0
IntIndex
Indices: array([0, 1, 2], dtype=int32)

[0, 1, 2]
Fill: 0
IntIndex
Indices: array([1, 2], dtype=int32)

What is unclear to me from reading the SparseArray code is whether SparseArray is permitted to contain fill_value values inside the sp_values array. The __init__ will filter out redundant values, unless provided a sparse_index object. In this case, it avoids re-doing the work of filtering redundant values, which can be quite slow in some cases.

I don't have much experience with Pandas's sparse implementation - I have only contributed to SciPy's sparse implementation. In the context of SciPy, it is entirely permitted to have 'explicit zeros' in the array. It is unclear to me if the bug here is that you can get a SparseArray that contains fill_value inside of sp_values, or the bug is that SparseArray.nonzero() contains code that assumes sp_values won't have any redundant values.

Playing around with SparseArray, it doesn't seem to be especially difficult to find ways to obtain a fill_value inside sp_values, even without abusing private APIs like the previous example.

For example, binops which result in fill_value can result in redundant values:

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

a = pd.arrays.SparseArray([True,  True,  True,  False])
b = pd.arrays.SparseArray([False, False, False, True])
print(a)
print(b)
result = a & b
print(result)

Output:

[True, True, True, False]
Fill: False
IntIndex
Indices: array([0, 1, 2], dtype=int32)

[False, False, False, True]
Fill: False
IntIndex
Indices: array([3], dtype=int32)

[False, False, False, False]
Fill: False
IntIndex
Indices: array([0, 1, 2, 3], dtype=int32)

In this example, all of the False values are being explicitly stored.

On the other hand, I did find a past Pandas issue that suggests a SparseArray in this state is not a valid value. That would imply that whatever methods you called in Pandas to obtain this SparseArray contain a bug somehow.

If you can identify the sequence of Pandas operations which resulted in a SparseArray which contains sp_value entries equal to fill_value, I would suggest following up with the Pandas developers.

Q: What is the correct syntax in Tampermonkey to point to a local audio file? A:

It is not on Tampermonkey's extension itself. It is on chrome's extension management options:

Right click on the Tampermonkey extension icon -> Manage extension / Manage add-on -> Allow scripts to access local files.

Q: How can I tell GitHub CoPilot CLI to always print clickable Urls? A:

Do you mean print the URLs out on the command line after building the application? I think this depends on the command line you are using. Are you using Bash, zsh, PowerShell, Windows Command (cmd.exe)?

Using Bash, echo 'https://stackoverflow.com' shows the URL, but it doesn't appear clickable until after I hold down the Ctrl key and hover my mouse cursor over the URL. Have you tried that?

Q: Forward host port to docker container A:

why not use slightly different solution, like this?

services:
  kubefwd:
    image: txn2/kubefwd
    command: ...
  app:
    image: bash
    command:
     - sleep
     - inf
    init: true
    network_mode: service:kubefwd

REF: txn2/kubefwd: Bulk port forwarding Kubernetes services for local development.
